source.title: Increasing Depth Leads to U-Shaped Test Risk in Over-parameterized Convolutional Networks
source.authors: Eshaan Nichani; Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan; C. Uhler

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plotted values are not given numerically in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly tests how test risk changes with depth in interpolating convolutional networks and reports a decreasing-then-increasing U-shaped curve, rather than a double-descent curve. This challenges the tested depth-based form of the claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own depth sweeps for ResNets, fully convolutional networks, CNTKs, and linear CNTKs. Results cited from other papers are not included as rows. Exact per-depth curve values are generally shown only in figures; the paper's explicit descriptions of those curves are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own depth sweeps on interpolating ResNets, fully-convolutional nets and CNTKs. It reports test risk falling, then rising, with no second descent past interpolation. This argues the model-wise double-descent form fails when capacity grows through depth.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find test risk U-shaped in depth for interpolating CNNs, in contrast to the post-interpolation decrease seen when increasing width. They explain this via the depth-dependent linear CNTK feature transformation: bias is lowest when it aligns with the true predictor, and variance is lowest when it matches the inverse data covariance.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps network depth, rather than testing the original double-descent claim's model-size, epoch, and sample-size curves. It also analyzes depth-dependent convolutional kernels and linear regression feature transformations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported depth trend is studied across architectures and settings, including ResNets of different widths, fully convolutional networks on different datasets and class counts, and CNTKs with different padding or pooling choices. Width-8 ResNets do not clearly show the increase and have not interpolated.

fits_no_version.finding: In linear CNTK regression on MNIST 0/1 (n=10), test loss is U-shaped in depth. It is minimized where the feature transformation best aligns with the true predictor. A bias–variance analysis shows variance is minimized when the transformation matches the inverse of the data covariance, and bias falls with alignment to the predictor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth acts as an inductive-bias (feature-alignment) parameter rather than capacity, giving a U-shaped risk at fixed parameter count.

record.problems: Most depth-curve outcomes are provided as figures without numerical values or reported error bars. Some experiments use only small subsets of the datasets; the CNTK experiment uses 250 examples each from two CIFAR10 classes, and the paper notes computational limits for larger CNTK runs. The width-8 ResNet does not interpolate, limiting its relevance to the interpolating-regime claim.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed plotted points for the depth sweeps and additional appendix variants (including alternate ResNet stage placements, kernel sizes, and some fully convolutional test-loss curves) are not listed separately because values are figure-only and the paper describes the same qualitative depth trend. Figures 9–10, 12, 14, 19–21, and the additional panels of Figures 16–23.

untested.parts: A width-axis peak near the interpolation threshold is not swept (only Fig 1a, width decrease, shown). No peak-then-descent is examined along depth beyond the tested range (up to depth 100 for ResNets).
Test risk over epochs is not measured.
Sample size is varied only to check that the depth U-shape is robust, not near a threshold.
Non-network model classes are not tested with a capacity axis crossing interpolation.
Label noise, multiple peaks and tuned regularization are not tested.

missing.what: Width sweep of interpolating ResNets on CIFAR10: test error decreases as width increases (own contrast to the depth result).
Increasing convolution kernel size in width-32 ResNet-10/18 raises test loss, another capacity axis with no second descent.
With 500 samples per class, the width-32 ResNet test loss still increases with depth.
Fully-Conv test cross-entropy loss also rises past a critical depth on all datasets.

record.verdict_notes: The paper treats depth as a capacity axis distinct from width. Its ResNets interpolate at all tested depths, so the interpolation threshold lies outside the depth range; the challenge is to continued improvement past interpolation, not to the peak. Fully-Conv 2/5-class runs do cross the threshold and keep degrading. All values are figure-only, with no error bars.

versions.untested_parts: Tests depth as the capacity axis, not width or other measures of model size; does not report a second descent at larger depths.
Training duration is stated, but test risk is not measured as a function of epochs.
A different sample count is used in an appendix experiment, but the study does not compare test error across sample sizes near an interpolation threshold.
Tests depth-dependent risk in convolutional networks and linear-kernel regression, not a general sweep across model classes and capacity measures.

Analyzes feature-transformation alignment and bias/variance in particular settings, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
Does not test whether label noise drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
Does not re-count complexity using an effective parameter measure or test whether that makes the curve an ordinary U-shape.
